entry.evidence: the focus has been exclusively on loads moving in a straight path, such as shown in Fig. 1

steps.action: Cite satellite SAR observations of vehicle-induced hydro-elastic waves on frozen lakes showing ship-wave-like patterns that agree with earlier theory.
steps.quote: Observations of such waves using satellite synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) imagery reveal ship-wave like patterns

steps.action: Cite earlier model results showing that a decelerating load can produce constructive wave interference exceeding the critical stress.
steps.quote: it was shown that a decelerating load could lead to constructive interference of waves which could exceed the critical stress

steps.action: Pose the question of how a curved load path changes the wave pattern and the strain in a floating ice sheet, motivated by ice-road safety.
steps.quote: we investigate the effect of a curved path on the waves created by the moving load

steps.action: Adopt the linearized fully dispersive hydro-elastic system (Dirichlet-Neumann operator form, with rotary inertia and damping) derived in the authors' earlier work.
steps.quote: The equations are derived in8 based on the approach used in24,25.

steps.action: Solve the system for an arbitrary load path with Laplace transform in time and Fourier transform in space, use a rotation-invariant Gaussian load, compute strain from the Hessian, and implement it with FFT and split path integrals.
steps.quote: The system can be solved using the Laplace transform

steps.action: Benchmark the computed centre-line strain for a straight-moving load against the published results of Shishmarev et al. (ref. 27), noting the different boundary conditions (Figure 2).
steps.quote: we compare the strain computed based on our solutions with the results obtained in27

steps.action: Choose a parameter set similar to field parameters (H = 6.8 m, h = 0.17 m, critical speed 6.0 m/s) and a supercritical load speed for the path illustrations.
steps.quote: we illustrate the response to various paths taken by a load moving at a super-critical speed

steps.action: Derive the dispersion relation of the undamped, unforced system and plot the phase speed, giving the minimum (critical) speed of 5.94 m/s (Appendix, Figure 7).
steps.quote: It is useful to look at the propagation of harmonic plane waves

steps.action: Compute the wave patterns for a straight path, a partly curved path, and a straight path followed by a full circle (Figures 3 and 4).
steps.quote: Then we display how the pattern changes when part of the path is curved

steps.action: Note in the model output that continued circling produces a quasi-steady outward-moving spiral wave pattern (Figure 5), left for further work.
steps.quote: a quasi-steady wave pattern emerges which appears to move outward in a spiral pattern

steps.action: Design an idealized ice-road scenario: a 1000 kg vehicle on 0.2 m ice decelerates from 35 to 14.4 km/h above a critical speed of 11.3 km/h, then turns (5 m or 40 m radius) or keeps decelerating on a straight path.
steps.quote: We consider an idealized case where a vehicle travels at a relatively high speed of 22 mph (35 km/h)

steps.action: Compute the maximum strain against time for each manoeuvre (Figure 6, right panel).
steps.quote: Maximum strain as a function of time for a 1000 kg vehicle continuing in a straight path and slowing down

steps.action: Vary the turning radius (30 to 90 m, and infinite) and tabulate the maximum strain, which peaks near 70 m and tends to the straight-path value (Table 1).
steps.quote: For the vehicle going into a turn, the maximal strain was computed for various vales of the radius.

steps.action: Compare the manoeuvres: large-radius turns give the highest and longest-lasting strain, a 5 m turn lowers strain but may be infeasible on ice, and stopping is safest.
steps.quote: the most dangerous action seems to be turning with a large radius

steps.action: Keep the claim that the model can be solved explicitly for a load on an arbitrary curved path with any load footprint.
steps.quote: It was shown how the model (2)–(3) can be solved explicitly for a load traveling in a curved path.

steps.action: Keep the claim that changes in direction can significantly affect strain, so slowing down followed by turning may be dangerous even in otherwise safe conditions.
steps.quote: it has been shown that changes in direction can have a significant effect on the strain in the ice

tree.answer: Known phenomenon: hydro-elastic ship-wave patterns from moving loads on ice
No: wave fields and strain under turning loads are computed, not measured
Describe how curved paths change wave patterns and strain, for ice-road safety
No rival hypotheses; alternative driver manoeuvres compared as scenarios
Yes: strain-time curves differ between straight deceleration and turns of different radius
Conditions set in the model (parameters, load paths)
Partly: one benchmark against ref. 27 and a turning-radius sweep; ice, depth and damping parameters not varied
Kept: turning, especially with a large radius, can raise maximum strain above straight-path deceleration

end.claim: The linear fully dispersive hydro-elastic model can be solved explicitly for loads on arbitrary curved paths; benchmarked against a published straight-path strain result, it shows that turning can raise ice strain above that of straight-path deceleration.

decisive_move.sentence: The Laplace-Fourier solution for a Gaussian load on an arbitrary path, with split path integrals, is what makes the curved-path wave and strain computations, and so every result, possible.

gates.evidence: No data were acquired; the simulations follow from the question about curved paths (§1 ¶7), not from a stated hypothesis. The method faced a benchmark against ref. 27 that it could have failed (§3 ¶6, Figure 2), but the safety claim (§4.2 ¶5) was not tested against any observation or rival model. Nothing is reported as fixed before the computations.

[...] contribution, we investigate the effect of a curved path on the waves created by the moving load.

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence. Headline status is capability_characterized (the method). Sub-claim: 'turning with a large radius is the most dangerous manoeuvre, with maximum strain near 70 m radius' is at best regularity_in_range, holding for one parameter set (1000 kg, h = 0.2 m, one depth and damping value); it was not compared with field data (inference). The benchmark against ref. 27 is qualitative ('line up quite well'), covers only the centre line and a straight path, and the two models use different boundary conditions; no benchmark exists for curved paths. Grid size, domain, time step and convergence are not reported. The damping coefficient b = 788 is given without justification. Caption and text are inconsistent: Figure 6 says the vehicle slows from 34 km/h, the text says 35 km/h; the plot shows an r = 20 m curve that the caption does not list; the deceleration unit is printed as m/s. Critical speeds of 5.94 m/s (Figure 1, Figure 7) and 6.0 m/s (§4.1 ¶1) are both used. The PDF caption of Table 1 states that the maximum lies near 70 m, but the XML caption is truncated. The 'exclusively straight path' claim rests on no stated literature search (inference). Composition none_fits: the walk is question-led model building, then one benchmark, scenario simulation and a parameter sweep, with no rivals, no observations and no frozen forecast, so neither capability_first (the question comes first) nor strong_inference applies.

disagreements.target: Earlier studies showing that a decelerating load can cause constructive interference and crack formation (refs. 8, 12)
disagreements.support: Simulated maximum strain for wide turns exceeds that of continued straight-path deceleration in the ice-road scenario (Figure 6, Table 1).
disagreements.quote: turning may also lead to constructive interference which may be more dangerous than slowing down.

disagreements.target: Operational ice-road safety practice (speed limits, Gold's formula load limits)
disagreements.support: In one idealized scenario, with a load conservative by Gold's formula, turning after deceleration raises the modelled strain; no failure threshold or field data are given.
disagreements.quote: slowing down followed by turning may in some cases be dangerous even in conditions which would be otherwise [...]
